notes:
Need to search first.I found commentary on 2 Samuel 3 from Enduring Word, the Pulpit Commentary, Matthew Henry, Jamieson-Fausset-Brown, Gill, Ellicott, Keil & Delitzsch, Coffman, the Expositor's Bible, Spurgeon and the NET Bible. The research tool hit its usage limit early. These notes therefore rely mostly on the search-result extracts of those pages, not full reads, and several verses have no coverage. Verses 6, 11, 20–21, 23, 26, 30, 32 and 34–35 are left out because I found nothing on them.

## 1. Traditional reading, verse by verse

**v. 1**
- **"Long war" means ongoing hostility, not constant battles.** Ellicott says Ish-bosheth was too weak to fight a real war. Neither side recognised the other, and David was willing to wait for God's promise to be fulfilled. Time worked for David because Ish-bosheth was clearly incompetent and people increasingly saw David as God's chosen king. Keil & Delitzsch say the same. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_samuel/3-1.htm
- **Gill:** the war went on about five more years as skirmishes, with people steadily defecting to David. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_samuel/3-1.htm
- **Pulpit Commentary:** since Ish-bosheth reigned only two years, Saul's house may have had a "puppet" representative after his death. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-samuel-3.html
- **Matthew Henry:** the long war tested David's faith and patience. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhc/2_samuel/3.htm
- **Spiritual applications.** Matthew Henry and Gill both compare the verse to grace growing stronger while corruption grows weaker in a believer. Gill also sees a picture of Christ's kingdom rising while antichrist's declines. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_samuel/3-1.htm

**vv. 2–5**
- **Why the list is here.** The Cambridge Bible says historians often insert a king's family at key moments, and the list shows David's house getting stronger. It notes that Amnon later fell into a sin that cost him his life. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_samuel/3-1.htm
- **Polygamy was wrong.** Matthew Henry calls David's many wives a fault against Deuteronomy 17:17 and a bad example to later kings. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/2Sa/2Sa_003.cfm
- Enduring Word also calls it a violation of Deuteronomy 17:17 and notes that Amnon, Absalom and Adonijah all brought trouble later. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-3/
- The Expositor's Bible says David sowed the seed of many sins and sorrows by multiplying wives. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/teb/2-samuel-3.html
- **Names and later history (Ellicott).** Chileab is called "Daniel" in 1 Chronicles 3:1. Adonijah later rebelled (1 Kings 1). Gill thinks Ahinoam was probably married to David before Abigail. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_samuel/3-2.htm
- **v. 3, Maacah:** JFB calls this a political marriage to win a northern ally. Piety gave way to policy, and the result was Absalom. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/2_samuel/3.htm
- **v. 5, Eglah:** Coffman says commentators are puzzled that only Eglah is called "David's wife." https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/2-samuel-3.html

**v. 7**
- **What the accusation meant.** Enduring Word says taking a royal concubine counted as both immorality and treason. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-3/
- JFB says it amounted to claiming the crown (compare 1 Kings 2:17), and it is unclear whether the charge was true. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/2_samuel/3.htm
- The Pulpit Commentary thinks Rizpah had probably lived apart from Ish-bosheth, so Abner may not have expected him to object. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/2_samuel/3.htm

**v. 8**
- **Was the charge false?** Enduring Word says Abner's reaction suggests it was. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-3/
- **Why Abner was so angry.** The Pulpit Commentary suggests the question was really a move to demote Abner, perhaps pushed by critics after his defeat at Gibeon. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/2_samuel/3.htm
- JFB says Abner valued his own services highly and bullied his weak nephew. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/2_samuel/3.htm

**vv. 9–10**
- **Abner knew God's purpose all along.** The Pulpit Commentary homilies say he must have been suppressing what he knew, and his oath condemns his own past conduct. G. Wood calls this "doing right wrongly": Abner knew David was God's choice yet caused years of needless bloodshed. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-samuel-3.html
- **God's purpose through bad motives.** Matthew Henry says ambition made Abner zealous for Ish-bosheth and revenge now made him zealous for David. Yet God used his anger for His own purposes. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/2Sa/2Sa_003.cfm
- **Dan to Beersheba** means north to south, the whole land. https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-samuel-3-commentary

**vv. 12–13**
- **Was David right to deal with Abner in secret?** JFB says his integrity can only be defended by the divine promise and his belief that Providence was using Abner's defection. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/2_samuel/3.htm
- JFB thinks David demanded Michal at that moment mainly to win over Saul's supporters, more than out of lingering love. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/2_samuel/3.htm
- **A different view.** Matthew Henry sees real generosity to Michal and to Saul's memory. He notes she had been separated from David partly by her father's authority. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhc/2_samuel/3.htm

**v. 14**
- **Why David asked Ish-bosheth directly.** The Pulpit Commentary says returning Michal had to be a public act of state. It was humiliating for Ish-bosheth, who had to reverse his father's decision and show he could not refuse David. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/2_samuel/3.htm
- **The hundred foreskins.** Coffman says David was naming the agreed price, not what he actually paid, so there is no conflict with 1 Samuel 18. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/2-samuel-3.html
- The NET notes say the Hebrew literally reads "whom I betrothed to myself." https://classic.net.bible.org/passage.php?passage=2sa+3:14-16

**vv. 15–16**
- **Paltiel.** The Pulpit Commentary says Abner stopped him at Bahurim, near the border of Judah. His fate was painful, but he had done wrong by marrying another man's wife, and David had suffered just as much when Michal was taken from him. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/2_samuel/3.htm

**vv. 17–19**
- **Timing.** Coffman, following Keil, treats this paragraph as a flashback describing what Abner had already done. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/2-samuel-3.html
- **No recorded promise.** Enduring Word notes there is no exact biblical record of the promise Abner quotes. It cites an older writer: Abner either heard it from Samuel's anointing of David or made it up. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-3/
- The Pulpit Commentary says Abner probably gave the popular reading of the prophecies. Calling David Israel's deliverer from the Philistines was meant to overcome prejudice against him, and Abner's speech admits his own failure against them. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/2_samuel/3.htm
- **Abner's motives.** JFB says he told the truth about David's calling but was hypocritical to claim religious motives when revenge drove him. Winning over Benjamin, Saul's tribe, was necessary policy. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/2_samuel/3.htm
- The Expositor's Bible says Abner, himself a Benjamite, was especially useful with that tribe. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/teb/2-samuel-3.html

**v. 22**
- **A criticism of David.** The Pulpit Commentary thinks David may have timed the raid so he could meet Abner while Joab was away. If David had acted openly, Joab might not have stood in the way. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/2_samuel/3.htm
- Coffman agrees and quotes R. Payne Smith on this. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/2-samuel-3.html

**vv. 24–25**
- **Joab's real concerns.** The Pulpit Commentary says he felt personally wronged and saw no room for both of them in the army, so he hid his own feelings behind zeal for the king. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/2_samuel/3.htm
- JFB says Joab may honestly have doubted Abner. But Abner was also a rival with great military talent, and there was the blood feud over Asahel. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/2_samuel/3.htm
- Enduring Word says Joab accused Abner of being a double agent, one of at least three reasons for his displeasure. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-3/
- The Pulpit Commentary homilies say Joab misunderstood David's peaceful policy and opposed it in his heart. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-samuel-3.html

**v. 27**
- **Location.** The Pulpit Commentary notes Hebron was a city of refuge (Joshua 20:7), which may be why Joab struck in the gate before Abner was inside. Treating this as the avenger-of-blood's right was "straining" the law, because Abner had killed in self-defence (Numbers 35). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/2_samuel/3.htm
- **Not a lawful blood-revenge.** Coffman, quoting another writer, calls it treacherous assassination that cannot be defended that way: Abner had warned Asahel repeatedly and killed him only to save his own life. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/2-samuel-3.html
- Matthew Henry says doing it openly in the gate made it worse, and it was also an attack on David. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/2Sa/2Sa_003.cfm
- The Pulpit Commentary homilies quote Hall: Ish-bosheth's wrong was now avenged by an enemy. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/homiletics/2_samuel/3.htm

**vv. 28–29**
- **The curse.** The Pulpit Commentary says David's curses were chosen to humiliate a gifted family. It also suggests from 1 Chronicles 11:6 that Joab lost his command for a time. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/2_samuel/3.htm
- The homilies say the curse was meant to show publicly what the crime deserved. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-samuel-3.html
- **Translation.** The NET has "one who works at the spindle" (women's work) where the BSB has "leans on a staff." https://classic.net.bible.org/verse.php?book=2Sa&chapter=3&verse=29

**v. 31**
- The Pulpit Commentary says "King David" is stressed because he walked in royal state, giving the funeral full dignity. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/2_samuel/3.htm

**v. 33**
- **"Fool" is *nabal*** (compare 1 Samuel 25:25 and Psalm 14:1). The Pulpit Commentary says it means worthlessness, not just silliness. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/2_samuel/3.htm
- **The lament.** Maclaren calls David following his old enemy's bier one of the most beautiful pictures in his life. Wordsworth calls the song a defence of both David and Abner. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/homiletics/2_samuel/3.htm

**vv. 36–37**
- **The funeral cleared David.** JFB says his conduct removed suspicion and turned opinion in his favour, more honourably than Abner's scheming would have. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/2_samuel/3.htm
- **But not fully.** The Pulpit Commentary says suspicion lingered and delayed David's reign over all Israel. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/2_samuel/3.htm
- Matthew Henry applies v. 36 to Christ: what He does pleases His willing people. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhc/2_samuel/3.htm

**v. 38**
- Matthew Henry says we should especially mourn useful men who fall while they are needed. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/2Sa/2Sa_003.cfm

**v. 39**
- **"Too hard for me."** Older commentators on the Biblehub page (Benson/Poole) say Joab and Abishai had so much power over the army and the people that David could not punish them without risk, especially while the other tribes still opposed him. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_samuel/3-39.htm
- Gill mentions another reading: "weak" may mean "tender" (merciful), unlike his harsh nephews. He prefers the first sense. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_samuel/3-39.htm
- The Pulpit Commentary says David had wanted Abner as a counterweight to Joab. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_samuel/3-39.htm
- **Critical view.** Matthew Henry says "carnal policy" spared Joab, and if justice had been done, later murders might have been prevented. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/2Sa/2Sa_003.cfm
- Enduring Word says David cursed Joab but did nothing to punish him. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-3/
- **Spurgeon's sermon** says David became "a time-server" for a while. He applies the verse to believers: the very strengths a person relies on can become hindrances. https://ccel.org/ccel/spurgeon/sermons06.xlvi.html

## 2. Protestant traditions that really differ
I found nothing. The commentators above (Gill and Spurgeon, both Baptist; Matthew Henry, a Nonconformist; JFB) agree on the main points. They differ only on details such as David's motive for demanding Michal. I found no Wesleyan, Lutheran or Pentecostal source on this chapter.

## 3. Other views
I found nothing on Catholic or Orthodox readings, modern scholarship (apart from the NET translation notes above), or popular modern teaching such as prosperity or word of faith. A Biblehub "Top 10 Lessons" page turned up, but I left it out because its quotations don't match the Bible text.

Before publishing, it would be worth re-reading the full pages for the URLs above (especially Enduring Word and Preceptaustin) to fill in the missing verses.
